claim: DIP2 is a conserved eukaryotic protein family found across Opisthokonta (fungi and animals).
source: We have recently identified a distant orthologue of FAALs as a part of a conserved three-domain protein called DIP2 across the eukaryotic supergroup Opisthokonta (fungi and animals) (Patil et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Patil et al., 2021

claim: Most opisthokonts have lost PKS/NRPS gene clusters.
source: However, paradoxically, most of the opisthokonts have lost PKS/NRPS gene cluster, suggesting the emergence of possible alternate functions of these FAAL orthologues.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Loss of CPS1 (a DIP2 orthologue) results in loss of virulence in plant pathogenic fungi causing rice blast and wheat head scab.
source: Recently, a loss of virulence has been reported when FAAL-like domain (FLD)-containing protein, CPS1, a DIP2 orthologue, is mutated in either plant pathogenic fungi, which causes rice blast and wheat head scab, or human pathogenic fungus, that cause valley fever (Lu et al., 2003; Narra et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 2003; Narra et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016

claim: Loss of CPS1 (a DIP2 orthologue) results in loss of virulence in human pathogenic fungus that causes valley fever.
source: Recently, a loss of virulence has been reported when FAAL-like domain (FLD)-containing protein, CPS1, a DIP2 orthologue, is mutated in either plant pathogenic fungi, which causes rice blast and wheat head scab, or human pathogenic fungus, that cause valley fever (Lu et al., 2003; Narra et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 2003; Narra et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016

claim: DIP2 is crucial for axonal branching in Drosophila.
source: Furthermore, DIP2 has been shown to be crucial for axonal branching, neurite sprouting, and dendritic spine morphogenesis in Drosophila, Caenorhabditis elegans, and mice, respectively (Ma et al., 2019a; Ma et al., 2019b; Sah et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2019a; Nitta et al., 2017; Noblett et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ma et al., 2019a; Ma et al., 2019b; Sah et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2019a; Nitta et al., 2017; Noblett et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2020

claim: DIP2 is crucial for neurite sprouting in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Furthermore, DIP2 has been shown to be crucial for axonal branching, neurite sprouting, and dendritic spine morphogenesis in Drosophila, Caenorhabditis elegans, and mice, respectively (Ma et al., 2019a; Ma et al., 2019b; Sah et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2019a; Nitta et al., 2017; Noblett et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ma et al., 2019a; Ma et al., 2019b; Sah et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2019a; Nitta et al., 2017; Noblett et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2020

claim: DIP2 is crucial for dendritic spine morphogenesis in mice.
source: Furthermore, DIP2 has been shown to be crucial for axonal branching, neurite sprouting, and dendritic spine morphogenesis in Drosophila, Caenorhabditis elegans, and mice, respectively (Ma et al., 2019a; Ma et al., 2019b; Sah et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2019a; Nitta et al., 2017; Noblett et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ma et al., 2019a; Ma et al., 2019b; Sah et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2019a; Nitta et al., 2017; Noblett et al., 2019; Xing et al., 2020

claim: Three paralogues of DIP2 in humans have been implicated as a potential risk factor for autism spectrum disorders (ASDs).
source: Three paralogues of DIP2 in humans have been implicated as a potential risk factor for neurodevelopmental disorders like autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) and other diseases (Egger et al., 2014; Gong et al., 2018; Iossifov et al., 2012; Jiao et al., 2012; Kong et al., 2016; Poelmans et al., 2009; Rudin et al., 2012; Larsson et al., 2017; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Egger et al., 2014; Gong et al., 2018; Iossifov et al., 2012; Jiao et al., 2012; Kong et al., 2016; Poelmans et al., 2009; Rudin et al., 2012; Larsson et al., 2017

claim: Prokaryotic FAALs were recruited early in eukaryotes along with PKS/NRPS systems in several Protozoa, Bikonta (mainly plants and algae), and Fungi.
source: The prokaryotic FAALs were recruited early in eukaryotes along with PKS/NRPS systems in several Protozoa, Bikonta (mainly plants and algae), and Fungi.
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis presented in the study

claim: A highly diverged FLD underwent duplication to produce a tandemly fused FLD didomain in all opisthokonts (except Basidiomycota fungi).
source: Subsequently, a highly diverged FLD went through the first duplication to produce a tandemly fused FLD didomain in all opisthokonts (except Basidiomycota fungi).
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis presented in the study

claim: A second duplication event occurred in vertebrates resulting in multiple paralogues of DIP2.
source: The second duplication event occurred in the vertebrates resulting in multiple paralogues of DIP2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis and shown in Figure 1A

claim: FLDs cluster with prokaryotic and plant FAALs but segregate as subclusters specific to FLD1 and FLD2.
source: Though FLDs cluster with prokaryotic and plant FAALs, they segregate as subclusters that are specific to FLD1 and FLD2 (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: Shown in phylogenetic tree in Figure 1B, C

claim: Both FLDs retain the ancestral motifs of the ANL superfamily while gaining exclusive variations in several motifs unique to each FLD.
source: Further analyses revealed that both the FLDs retain the ancestral motifs of the ANL superfamily (Gulick, 2009) while gaining exclusive variations in several motifs, unique to each FLD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and supported by citation to Gulick, 2009

claim: Cmr2 (ScDIP2) shares an average sequence identity of ~19% with other DIP2 proteins.
source: For instance, Cmr2 (YOR093c), the yeast orthologue of DIP2 (hereafter referred to as ScDIP2), shares an average sequence identity of ~19% (~16–27%) with other DIP2 proteins.
evidence: Calculated from sequence analysis

claim: ∆ScDIP2 cells show a significant ~23% increase in total DAG level compared to wild type.
source: ∆ScDIP2 cells showed a significant ~23% increase in the total DAG level compared to the wild type (Figure 1E) with a moderate depletion in TAG level (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Measured by radio-TLC and shown in Figure 1E

claim: ∆ScDIP2 cells show a moderate depletion in TAG level.
source: ∆ScDIP2 cells showed a significant ~23% increase in the total DAG level compared to the wild type (Figure 1E) with a moderate depletion in TAG level (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Measured by radio-TLC and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D

claim: None of the other membrane lipid classes showed any significant change in ∆ScDIP2 cells.
source: However, none of the other membrane lipid classes showed any significant change (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Measured by radio-TLC and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D

claim: ΔDmDIP2 Drosophila show ~twofold accumulation in a subset of DAG species compared to wild type.
source: A comparative liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS) analysis of whole-tissue lipid extracts from adult wild type (Canton-S) and ΔDmDIP2 Drosophila showed ~twofold accumulation in a subset of DAG species (Figure 1F).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 1F

claim: ΔMmDIP2A mouse ES cells show ~3- to 12-fold accumulation of DAG species compared to wild-type ES cells.
source: Interestingly, the absence of even a single paralogue, DIP2A in the ES cells isolated from ΔMmDIP2A mice, showed ~3- to 12-fold accumulation of DAG species compared to wild-type ES cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 1G

claim: ΔDmDIP2 flies show preferential accumulation of C16 acyl chain-containing subset of DAGs (C32:0, C32:1, C34:0, C34:1).
source: We noted a preferential accumulation of C16 acyl chain-containing subset of DAGs (C32:0, C32:1, C34:0, C34:1) in ΔDmDIP2 flies, while the accumulation is biased towards C32:1, C36:1, and C36:2 DAGs in ΔMmDIP2A ES cells (fold change indicated in Figure 1F, G).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 1F

claim: ΔMmDIP2A ES cells show accumulation biased towards C32:1, C36:1, and C36:2 DAGs.
source: We noted a preferential accumulation of C16 acyl chain-containing subset of DAGs (C32:0, C32:1, C34:0, C34:1) in ΔDmDIP2 flies, while the accumulation is biased towards C32:1, C36:1, and C36:2 DAGs in ΔMmDIP2A ES cells (fold change indicated in Figure 1F, G).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 1G

claim: ΔScDIP2 strain shows ~19-fold accumulation of C36:0 DAG subspecies.
source: LC–MS analysis of yeast lipidome revealed a striking ~19-fold accumulation of C36:0 and ~8-fold accumulation of C36:1 chain-length DAG subspecies in ΔScDIP2 strain (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 2A

claim: ΔScDIP2 strain shows ~8-fold accumulation of C36:1 DAG subspecies.
source: LC–MS analysis of yeast lipidome revealed a striking ~19-fold accumulation of C36:0 and ~8-fold accumulation of C36:1 chain-length DAG subspecies in ΔScDIP2 strain (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 2A

claim: Genetic complementation with ScDIP2 under native or galactose-inducible promoters restored the levels of DAGs in ΔScDIP2.
source: Genetic complementation with ScDIP2 under native or galactose-inducible (with a C-terminal GFP tag) promoters restored the levels of DAGs (Figure 2B).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 2B

claim: The abundant DAG species (representing >90% of total DAG pool), comprised of C32 and C34 chain lengths, remained unchanged in ∆ScDIP2.
source: To our surprise, the abundant DAG species (representing >90% of total DAG pool), comprised of C32 and C34 chain lengths (Casanovas et al., 2015; Ejsing et al., 2009), hereafter referred to as bulk DAG pool, remained unchanged in ∆ScDIP2.
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and supported by citations to Casanovas et al., 2015; Ejsing et al., 2009

claim: The DAG subspecies accumulation in ∆ScDIP2 is independent of the well-characterized bulk DAG metabolizing pathways through Dga1, Lro1, Are1, Are2, and Dgk1.
source: Interestingly, this indicates that the DAG subspecies accumulation is independent of the well-characterized bulk DAG metabolizing pathways through Dga1, Lro1, Are1, Are2 (DAG acyltransferases), and Dgk1 (DAG kinase) (Li et al., 2020; Rockenfeller et al., 2018).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that bulk DAGs remain unchanged and supported by citations to Li et al., 2020; Rockenfeller et al., 2018

claim: Deletion of ScDIP2 resulted in depletion of ~30-40% TAGs related to a defined subset of DAGs (C36:0 and C36:1).
source: Lipidomics revealed a depletion of ~30–40% TAGs related to a defined subset of DAGs (C36:0 and C36:1), with the highest depletion of ~93% in the case of C18:0/36:1 TAG (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 2C

claim: C18:0/36:1 TAG showed the highest depletion of ~93% in ΔScDIP2.
source: Lipidomics revealed a depletion of ~30–40% TAGs related to a defined subset of DAGs (C36:0 and C36:1), with the highest depletion of ~93% in the case of C18:0/36:1 TAG (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 2C

claim: The levels of FFAs, MAGs and glycerol were found to be unaltered in the ΔScDIP2 cells when compared to wild-type cells.
source: The levels of FFAs, monoacylglycerols (MAGs) and glycerol were found to be unaltered in the ΔScDIP2cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–D) when compared to the wild-type cells.
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–D

claim: Increased lipolysis is unlikely to have been the cause for DAG–TAG imbalance in ΔScDIP2.
source: It clearly suggests that increased lipolysis is unlikely to have been the cause for DAG–TAG imbalance.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that FFAs, MAGs, and glycerol levels are unchanged

claim: ScDIP2 is involved in selective DAG to TAG flux, possibly by direct or indirect facilitation of an acylation reaction of DAG subspecies.
source: Taken together, the results suggest that ScDIP2 is involved in selective DAG to TAG flux, possibly by direct or indirect facilitation of an acylation reaction of DAG subspecies (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that DAGs accumulate and TAGs deplete in the mutant

claim: The depletion of TAG levels in ΔMmDIP2A mouse ES cell lines is consistent with the role of DIP2 in DAG to TAG conversion.
source: The depletion of TAG levels in ΔMmDIP2A mouse ES cell lines is in consensus with this argument (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A

claim: The TAG levels of ΔDmDIP2 Drosophila remained comparable to wild type.
source: However, it should be noted that the TAG levels of ΔDmDIP2 Drosophila remained comparable to wild type (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), which perhaps could be attributed to a masking effect from the huge amount of TAG sourced from the fat body of Drosophila (Heier and Kühnlein, 2018).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, with citation to Heier and Kühnlein, 2018

claim: C18:1/36:0 TAG increased by ~122% in ScDIP2-OE cells.
source: We found that the TAGs related to selective DAGs, C18:1/36:0 TAG increased the most (~122%), while C18:0/36:1 and C18:0/36:2 TAG increased by ~58% and ~80%, respectively in ScDIP2-OE cells (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 2D

claim: C18:0/36:1 TAG increased by ~58% in ScDIP2-OE cells.
source: We found that the TAGs related to selective DAGs, C18:1/36:0 TAG increased the most (~122%), while C18:0/36:1 and C18:0/36:2 TAG increased by ~58% and ~80%, respectively in ScDIP2-OE cells (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 2D

claim: C18:0/36:2 TAG increased by ~80% in ScDIP2-OE cells.
source: We found that the TAGs related to selective DAGs, C18:1/36:0 TAG increased the most (~122%), while C18:0/36:1 and C18:0/36:2 TAG increased by ~58% and ~80%, respectively in ScDIP2-OE cells (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 2D

claim: C36:1 DAG showed the highest fold change (~10-fold) in depletion in ScDIP2-OE cells.
source: Concomitantly, selective DAG species, C36:1 DAG showed the highest fold change (~10-fold) in depletion, further below the basal level in ScDIP2-OE cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 2E

claim: DIP2 expression is crucial to maintain the basal level of DAG subspecies and directly facilitates a DAG to TAG conversion process.
source: Therefore, the data suggest that the DIP2 expression is crucial to maintain the basal level of DAG subspecies and directly facilitates a DAG to TAG conversion process (Figure 2F).
evidence: Inferred from overexpression and deletion experiments

claim: ∆ScDIP2 cells showed normal growth under standard nutrient conditions.
source: As ∆ScDIP2 cells showed normal growth and no distinct morphological defects under standard nutrient conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B), we assessed its adaptability to different stress conditions such as nutrient deficiency, osmotic stress, temperature changes, redox stress to name a few (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Measured by growth curve and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: ∆ScDIP2 cells showed no distinct morphological defects under standard nutrient conditions.
source: As ∆ScDIP2 cells showed normal growth and no distinct morphological defects under standard nutrient conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B), we assessed its adaptability to different stress conditions such as nutrient deficiency, osmotic stress, temperature changes, redox stress to name a few (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Observed by microscopy and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: ∆ScDIP2 cells showed significant growth impairment in the presence of tunicamycin.
source: ∆ScDIP2 cells showed significant growth impairment in the presence of tunicamycin (Figure 3A), which was earlier observed in a genome-wide screen (Chen et al., 2005).
evidence: Measured by serial dilution assay and shown in Figure 3A, with citation to Chen et al., 2005

claim: Tunicamycin is an inhibitor of N-linked glycosylation in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: Tunicamycin, an inhibitor of N-linked glycosylation in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), induces misfolded protein accumulation in ER lumen leading to proteostasis defect, commonly referred to as 'ER stress'.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field

claim: Tunicamycin induces misfolded protein accumulation in ER lumen leading to proteostasis defect, commonly referred to as 'ER stress'.
source: Tunicamycin, an inhibitor of N-linked glycosylation in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), induces misfolded protein accumulation in ER lumen leading to proteostasis defect, commonly referred to as 'ER stress'.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field

claim: Genetic complementation using native promoter was sufficient to rescue tunicamycin-induced ER stress in ΔScDIP2.
source: Genetic complementation using native promoter (Figure 3A) or GAL1 promoter (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B) was sufficient to rescue tunicamycin-induced ER stress.
evidence: Measured by serial dilution assay and shown in Figure 3A

claim: Genetic complementation using GAL1 promoter was sufficient to rescue tunicamycin-induced ER stress in ΔScDIP2.
source: Genetic complementation using native promoter (Figure 3A) or GAL1 promoter (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B) was sufficient to rescue tunicamycin-induced ER stress.
evidence: Measured by serial dilution assay and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B

claim: ER stress is known to activate UPR signalling, a highly conserved homeostasis signalling in all eukaryotes.
source: ER stress is known to activate UPR signalling, a highly conserved homeostasis signalling in all eukaryotes (Han et al., 2010; Ron and Walter, 2007).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations to Han et al., 2010; Ron and Walter, 2007

claim: ΔScDIP2 cells exhibited a ~1.6-fold elevated UPR stress than basal levels found in wild type.
source: ΔScDIP2 cells exhibited a ~1.6-fold elevated UPR stress than basal levels found in wild type (Figure 3B) and the addition of tunicamycin only exacerbated the already active ER stress in the mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Measured by FACS-based UPR reporter assay and shown in Figure 3B

claim: The addition of tunicamycin exacerbated the already active ER stress in the ΔScDIP2 mutant.
source: ΔScDIP2 cells exhibited a ~1.6-fold elevated UPR stress than basal levels found in wild type (Figure 3B) and the addition of tunicamycin only exacerbated the already active ER stress in the mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Measured by FACS-based UPR reporter assay and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F

claim: The ΔScDIP2 mutant suffers from ER stress even in the absence of stress-inducing agents.
source: It implies that the mutant suffers from ER stress even in the absence of stress-inducing agents.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that UPR is elevated in the mutant without tunicamycin treatment

claim: Oleic acid (OL; C18:1 FFA) supplementation rescued the ER stress phenotype in ∆ScDIP2 cells.
source: We found that except for oleic acid (OL; C18:1 FFA), none of the other precursors rescued the ER stress phenotype (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Measured by serial dilution assay and shown in Figure 3C

claim: Choline supplementation did not rescue the ER stress phenotype in ∆ScDIP2 cells.
source: We found that except for oleic acid (OL; C18:1 FFA), none of the other precursors rescued the ER stress phenotype (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Measured by serial dilution assay and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C

claim: Ethanolamine supplementation did not rescue the ER stress phenotype in ∆ScDIP2 cells.
source: We found that except for oleic acid (OL; C18:1 FFA), none of the other precursors rescued the ER stress phenotype (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Measured by serial dilution assay and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C

claim: Palmitoleic acid (C16:1 FFA) supplementation did not relieve ER stress in ∆ScDIP2 mutants.
source: The supplementation of ∆ScDIP2 mutants with a different unsaturated FA (e.g. palmitoleic acid; C16:1 FFA) or saturated FA (e.g.: palmitic acid; C16:0 FFA, stearic acid; C18:0 FFA) did not relieve ER stress (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Measured by serial dilution assay and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D

claim: Palmitic acid (C16:0 FFA) supplementation did not relieve ER stress in ∆ScDIP2 mutants.
source: The supplementation of ∆ScDIP2 mutants with a different unsaturated FA (e.g. palmitoleic acid; C16:1 FFA) or saturated FA (e.g.: palmitic acid; C16:0 FFA, stearic acid; C18:0 FFA) did not relieve ER stress (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Measured by serial dilution assay and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D

claim: Stearic acid (C18:0 FFA) supplementation did not relieve ER stress in ∆ScDIP2 mutants.
source: The supplementation of ∆ScDIP2 mutants with a different unsaturated FA (e.g. palmitoleic acid; C16:1 FFA) or saturated FA (e.g.: palmitic acid; C16:0 FFA, stearic acid; C18:0 FFA) did not relieve ER stress (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Measured by serial dilution assay and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D

claim: OL supplementation was enough to reduce the constitutive UPR upregulation in ∆ScDIP2.
source: Furthermore, OL supplementation was enough to reduce the constitutive UPR upregulation in ∆ScDIP2 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Measured by FACS-based UPR reporter assay and shown in Figure 3D

claim: OL supplementation restored the accumulated subset of DAGs back to basal levels in ∆ScDIP2.
source: In agreement with those observations, the LC–MS analysis revealed the restoration of the accumulated subset of DAGs back to basal levels (Figure 3E).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 3E

claim: OL supplementation resulted in normalization of related TAG subspecies in ∆ScDIP2.
source: A concomitant normalization in related TAG subspecies (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2F) was also observed upon OL supplementation along with an overall ~three- to sevenfold increase in bulk TAG production (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 3F

claim: OL supplementation resulted in an overall ~three- to sevenfold increase in bulk TAG production in ∆ScDIP2.
source: A concomitant normalization in related TAG subspecies (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2F) was also observed upon OL supplementation along with an overall ~three- to sevenfold increase in bulk TAG production (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G

claim: Null mutants of canonical DAG-utilizing enzymes such as Dga1 and Lro1 or Dgk1 are not sensitive to ER stress.
source: It is interesting to note that bulk DAG accumulation is possibly less toxic to ER as the null mutants of canonical DAG-utilizing enzymes such as Dga1 and Lro1 or Dgk1 are not sensitive to ER stress (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Measured by serial dilution assay and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Bulk DAG accumulation is possibly less toxic to ER than selective DAG accumulation.
source: It is interesting to note that bulk DAG accumulation is possibly less toxic to ER as the null mutants of canonical DAG-utilizing enzymes such as Dga1 and Lro1 or Dgk1 are not sensitive to ER stress (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mutants with bulk DAG accumulation are not sensitive to ER stress

claim: ScDIP2 alleviates the ER stress by facilitating the buffering of selective DAGs from the membrane pool to the storage pool.
source: This indicates the atypical role of selective DAG subspecies as their accumulation results in ER stress, while ScDIP2 alleviates the ER stress by facilitating the buffering of such DAGs from the membrane pool to the storage pool (Figure 3G).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that OL supplementation restores DAG levels and relieves ER stress

claim: Under nutrient limitation conditions such as stationary phase, yeast is known to massively upregulate endogenous OL production and subsequent TAG synthesis.
source: Under nutrient limitation conditions such as stationary phase, yeast is known to massively upregulate endogenous OL production and subsequent TAG synthesis, facilitated by majorly Dga1 and Lro1, as a metabolic strategy to store energy in the form of neutral lipids (Casanovas et al., 2015; Jacquier et al., 2011; Joshi et al., 2018; Markgraf et al., 2014).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations to Casanovas et al., 2015; Jacquier et al., 2011; Joshi et al., 2018; Markgraf et al., 2014

claim: The bulk DAG levels across the various stages of growth phases remain constant in the wild type.
source: The bulk DAG levels across the various stages of growth phases remain constant in the wild type, which was also observed in earlier reports (Casanovas et al., 2015).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and supported by citation to Casanovas et al., 2015

claim: The ∆ScDIP2 cells showed the accumulation of a selective subset of DAGs only during the early- and mid-log phase.
source: Strikingly, the ∆ScDIP2 cells showed the accumulation of a selective subset of DAGs only during the early- and mid-log phase and these levels are restored during the stationary phase (Figure 4A).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 4A

claim: The selective DAG levels in ∆ScDIP2 cells are restored during the stationary phase.
source: Strikingly, the ∆ScDIP2 cells showed the accumulation of a selective subset of DAGs only during the early- and mid-log phase and these levels are restored during the stationary phase (Figure 4A).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 4A

claim: The toxic accumulation of selective DAGs is diluted by the bulk conversion of DAGs to TAGs during the stationary phase.
source: Thus, the toxic accumulation of selective DAGs is diluted by the bulk conversion of DAGs to TAGs during the stationary phase, which also suppress the activated UPR (Figure 4B).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that DAG levels are restored and UPR is reduced in stationary phase

claim: The activated UPR in ∆ScDIP2 is suppressed during the stationary phase.
source: Thus, the toxic accumulation of selective DAGs is diluted by the bulk conversion of DAGs to TAGs during the stationary phase, which also suppress the activated UPR (Figure 4B).
evidence: Measured by FACS-based UPR reporter assay and shown in Figure 4B

claim: The expression of ScDIP2-GFP appeared as an intracellular tubular and punctate-like structure only during the early- to mid-log phase.
source: The expression of ScDIP2-GFP appeared as an intracellular tubular and punctate-like structure only during the early- to mid-log phase and rapidly diminished in the stationary phase (Figure 4C).
evidence: Observed by fluorescence microscopy and shown in Figure 4C

claim: The expression of ScDIP2-GFP rapidly diminished in the stationary phase.
source: The expression of ScDIP2-GFP appeared as an intracellular tubular and punctate-like structure only during the early- to mid-log phase and rapidly diminished in the stationary phase (Figure 4C).
evidence: Observed by fluorescence microscopy and shown in Figure 4C

claim: The role of ScDIP2 in regulating a defined subset of DAGs to TAG flux is a growth phase-dependent phenomenon.
source: It is, therefore, evident that the role of ScDIP2 in regulating a defined subset of DAGs to TAG flux must be a growth phase-dependent phenomenon.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ScDIP2 expression and DAG accumulation are growth phase-dependent

claim: ScDIP2-GFP signal was found to be primarily colocalized with the mitochondrial marker, MitoTracker.
source: Using fluorescence microscopy, ScDIP2-GFP signal was found to be primarily colocalized with the mitochondrial marker, MitoTracker (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Observed by fluorescence microscopy and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B

claim: Mitochondrial colocalization of mouse DIP2A in a mammalian cell line has been reported previously.
source: This observation was also supported by previous reports on mitochondrial colocalization of mouse DIP2A in a mammalian cell line and its role in superoxide dismutase-mediated antioxidative response (Bai et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bai et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2019a

claim: Mouse DIP2A has a role in superoxide dismutase-mediated antioxidative response.
source: This observation was also supported by previous reports on mitochondrial colocalization of mouse DIP2A in a mammalian cell line and its role in superoxide dismutase-mediated antioxidative response (Bai et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bai et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2019a

claim: A partial association of ScDIP2-GFP puncta with vacuolar surface stained with FM4-64 dye was observed.
source: Interestingly, we also observed a partial association of ScDIP2-GFP puncta with vacuolar surface stained with FM4-64 dye (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D; see also Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–M).
evidence: Observed by fluorescence microscopy and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D

claim: 30–40% of ScDIP2-GFP puncta overlapped with vacuolar marker.
source: A quantification of colocalization revealed that 30–40% of ScDIP2-GFP puncta (fluorescence signal) overlapped with vacuolar marker and 70–80% signal overlapped with mitochondrial marker (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: Quantified from fluorescence microscopy images and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, G

claim: 70–80% of ScDIP2-GFP signal overlapped with mitochondrial marker.
source: A quantification of colocalization revealed that 30–40% of ScDIP2-GFP puncta (fluorescence signal) overlapped with vacuolar marker and 70–80% signal overlapped with mitochondrial marker (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: Quantified from fluorescence microscopy images and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, G

claim: A fraction of ScDIP2-GFP puncta (~30%) was associated with both the vacuolar and mitochondrial marker signal.
source: Subsequently, a three-colour colocalization study of ScDIP2-GFP (green), mitochondria (4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI); blue) (Dellinger and Gèze, 2001; Higuchi-Sanabria et al., 2016; Zarin et al., 2021), and vacuoles (FM4-64; red) showed that a fraction of ScDIP2-GFP puncta (~30%) was associated with both the vacuolar and mitochondrial marker signal (Figure 5A, B; Figure 5—figure supplement 11H, 1I).
evidence: Quantified from fluorescence microscopy images and shown in Figure 5A, B

claim: All the vacuole-associated ScDIP2 puncta overlap with mitochondrial marker (DAPI).
source: While the major fraction of ScDIP2-GFP puncta localizes to mitochondria, all the vacuole-associated ScDIP2 puncta overlap with mitochondrial marker (DAPI), suggesting that the vacuolar association of ScDIP2 is at the mitochondrial–vacuolar contact site.
evidence: Observed from fluorescence microscopy images

claim: The vacuolar association of ScDIP2 is at the mitochondrial–vacuolar contact site.
source: While the major fraction of ScDIP2-GFP puncta localizes to mitochondria, all the vacuole-associated ScDIP2 puncta overlap with mitochondrial marker (DAPI), suggesting that the vacuolar association of ScDIP2 is at the mitochondrial–vacuolar contact site.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that all vacuole-associated ScDIP2 puncta overlap with mitochondrial marker

claim: ScDIP2 interacts with vacuole–mitochondria contact site (vCLAMP) protein, Vps39.
source: The localization of ScDIP2 at mitochondria–vacuole contact site is further supported by a previous study showing its interaction with vacuole–mitochondria contact site (vCLAMP) protein, Vps39 (Elbaz-Alon et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Elbaz-Alon et al., 2014

claim: About 60% of ΔScDIP2 cells contain a greater number of single, rounded, and enlarged vacuoles, which is roughly twice that of the wild type.
source: We found that about 60% of ΔScDIP2 cells contain a greater number of single, rounded, and enlarged vacuoles, which is roughly twice that of the wild type (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: Quantified from fluorescence microscopy images and shown in Figure 5C, D

claim: Larger sized vacuoles are more frequently observed in ΔScDIP2 mutant than the wild type.
source: A comparative analysis of the size distribution of vacuoles in the log phase of growth showed that larger sized vacuoles are more frequently observed in ΔScDIP2 mutant than the wild type (Figure 5E).
evidence: Quantified from fluorescence microscopy images and shown in Figure 5E

claim: The increase of single and large vacuoles in ΔScDIP2 cells is presumably due to aberrant vacuole membrane fusion driven by accumulated DAGs.
source: Thus, the increase of single and large vacuoles in ΔScDIP2 cells is presumably due to aberrant vacuole membrane fusion driven by accumulated DAGs, a known membrane fusogen (Starr and Fratti, 2019).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of enlarged vacuoles and supported by citation to Starr and Fratti, 2019

claim: DAGs are known membrane fusogens.
source: Thus, the increase of single and large vacuoles in ΔScDIP2 cells is presumably due to aberrant vacuole membrane fusion driven by accumulated DAGs, a known membrane fusogen (Starr and Fratti, 2019).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation to Starr and Fratti, 2019

claim: Optimum vacuole fusion is critical for cells' adaptation to osmotic stress.
source: The optimum vacuole fusion is critical for cells' adaptation to osmotic stress, a common environmental stress experience by fungi (Veses et al., 2008), To check the functional consequence of such compromised vacuolar homeostasis, ΔScDIP2 cells were subjected to hyper-osmotic stress using high-salt growth media.
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation to Veses et al., 2008

claim: Incubation in hyper-osmotic conditions resulted in two- to threefold higher cell death in ΔScDIP2 compared to wild type.
source: An incubation in hyper-osmotic conditions resulted in two- to threefold higher cell death in ΔScDIP2, while the cell viability was identical for both the strains in the absence of stress (Figure 5F).
evidence: Measured by trypan blue staining and shown in Figure 5F

claim: Cell viability was identical for wild type and ΔScDIP2 strains in the absence of osmotic stress.
source: An incubation in hyper-osmotic conditions resulted in two- to threefold higher cell death in ΔScDIP2, while the cell viability was identical for both the strains in the absence of stress (Figure 5F).
evidence: Measured by trypan blue staining and shown in Figure 5F

claim: The vacuoles in the ScDIP2-OE strain were found to be highly fragmented.
source: The vacuoles in the ScDIP2-OE strain were found to be highly fragmented; single vacuole containing cells are about three times lower while the multivacuolar (>4) cells were three times more than that in the wild type (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: Observed by fluorescence microscopy and shown in Figure 6A, B

claim: Single vacuole containing cells are about three times lower in ScDIP2-OE compared to wild type.
source: The vacuoles in the ScDIP2-OE strain were found to be highly fragmented; single vacuole containing cells are about three times lower while the multivacuolar (>4) cells were three times more than that in the wild type (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: Quantified from fluorescence microscopy images and shown in Figure 6A, B

claim: Multivacuolar (>4) cells were three times more in ScDIP2-OE than in wild type.
source: The vacuoles in the ScDIP2-OE strain were found to be highly fragmented; single vacuole containing cells are about three times lower while the multivacuolar (>4) cells were three times more than that in the wild type (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: Quantified from fluorescence microscopy images and shown in Figure 6A, B

claim: Growth in hypertonic media induces vacuole fission in yeast.
source: The growth in hypertonic media induces vacuole fission in yeast, resulting in highly fragmented vacuoles in both wild-type and ScDIP2-OE cells (Figure 6D, E).
evidence: Established knowledge and observed in Figure 6D, E

claim: Exposure of cells with fragmented vacuoles to hypotonic conditions induces rapid vacuole fusion.
source: Exposure of such cells with fragmented vacuoles to hypotonic conditions induces rapid vacuole fusion.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field

claim: Vacuoles in ScDIP2-OE cells are highly fragmented and multilobar even after the fusion induction using hypotonic media.
source: Vacuoles in ScDIP2-OE cells are found to be highly fragmented and multilobar even after the fusion induction using hypotonic media (Figure 6F), suggesting a significantly reduced vacuolar fusion process (~30% reduced fusion compared to wild type) (Figure 6G).
evidence: Observed by fluorescence microscopy and shown in Figure 6F

claim: ScDIP2-OE cells show ~30% reduced vacuolar fusion compared to wild type.
source: Vacuoles in ScDIP2-OE cells are found to be highly fragmented and multilobar even after the fusion induction using hypotonic media (Figure 6F), suggesting a significantly reduced vacuolar fusion process (~30% reduced fusion compared to wild type) (Figure 6G).
evidence: Quantified from fluorescence microscopy images and shown in Figure 6G

claim: Rapid vacuole fusion is required during hypo-osmotic stress adaptation by yeast cells.
source: Since rapid vacuole fusion is required during hypo-osmotic stress adaptation by yeast cells, we hypothesized that ScDIP2-OE cells will show reduced fitness in hypotonic conditions.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field

claim: Acute hypotonic stress caused severe cell death in ScDIP2-OE.
source: Indeed, we found that acute hypotonic stress caused severe cell death in ScDIP2-OE while ∆ScDIP2 cells showed significant tolerance to the stress compared to the wildtype (Figure 6H).
evidence: Measured by trypan blue staining and shown in Figure 6H

claim: ∆ScDIP2 cells showed significant tolerance to hypotonic stress compared to wild type.
source: Indeed, we found that acute hypotonic stress caused severe cell death in ScDIP2-OE while ∆ScDIP2 cells showed significant tolerance to the stress compared to the wildtype (Figure 6H).
evidence: Measured by trypan blue staining and shown in Figure 6H

claim: The selective DAG pool is essential for the vacuole fusion process.
source: Together, the data suggest that the selective DAG pool is essential for the vacuole fusion process and ScDIP2-mediated regulation optimizes the process to ensure osmoadaptation in yeast.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that DAG depletion reduces vacuole fusion

claim: ScDIP2-mediated regulation optimizes the vacuole fusion process to ensure osmoadaptation in yeast.
source: Together, the data suggest that the selective DAG pool is essential for the vacuole fusion process and ScDIP2-mediated regulation optimizes the process to ensure osmoadaptation in yeast.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both loss and overexpression of ScDIP2 impair osmoadaptation

claim: The N-terminal DMAP1-binding domain (DBD1) is absent in several ancient members of Opisthokonta.
source: Bioinformatics analysis on the emergence of the unique three-domain architecture of DIP2 in opisthokonts revealed that the N-terminal DMAP1-binding domain (DBD1) is absent in several ancient members of this group (viz. Nucleariids, Ichthyosporea, Choanoflagellates, and some fungi species).
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis

claim: The tandem FLD-didomain (FLD1–FLD2) architecture is conserved throughout all opisthokonts.
source: However, the tandem FLD-didomain (FLD1–FLD2) architecture is conserved throughout all opisthokonts (Figure 7A).
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis and shown in Figure 7A

claim: Tandem FLD didomain is minimally required to prevent ER stress in ΔScDIP2.
source: The genetic complementation assay with multiple domain-truncated constructs revealed that tandem FLD didomain is minimally required to prevent ER stress, while the DBD1 is dispensable (Figure 7B).
evidence: Measured by serial dilution assay and shown in Figure 7B

claim: DBD1 is dispensable for preventing ER stress in ΔScDIP2.
source: The genetic complementation assay with multiple domain-truncated constructs revealed that tandem FLD didomain is minimally required to prevent ER stress, while the DBD1 is dispensable (Figure 7B).
evidence: Measured by serial dilution assay and shown in Figure 7B

claim: The FLD didomain restored the levels of the subset of DAGs characteristic to yeast.
source: We found that the FLD didomain restored the levels of the subset of DAGs characteristic to yeast (Figure 7C), accompanied by the generation of related TAGs (Figure 7D).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 7C

claim: The FLD didomain restored the generation of related TAGs in ΔScDIP2.
source: We found that the FLD didomain restored the levels of the subset of DAGs characteristic to yeast (Figure 7C), accompanied by the generation of related TAGs (Figure 7D).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 7D

claim: Restoration of the DAG level is not evident when either of the FLDs is missing.
source: Such a restoration of the DAG level is not evident when either of the FLDs is missing (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C

claim: The recruitment and duplication of FLDs was an innovation in early Opisthokonta evolution to tackle a specific fraction of the DAGs pool.
source: These results suggest that the recruitment and duplication of FLDs was an innovation in early Opisthokonta evolution to tackle a specific fraction of the DAGs pool, which if accumulated may become toxic.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that FLD didomain is required for DAG regulation

claim: The A5 and A7 motifs are conserved in the FLD1 domains of all opisthokonts.
source: Structure-based sequence alignments, using models from AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (Jumper et al., 2021; Varadi et al., 2022), suggested that the A5 and A7 motifs are conserved in the FLD1 domains of all opisthokonts (Figure 7E) and strikingly, FLD2 showed degeneration of both the motifs.
evidence: Inferred from sequence alignment and shown in Figure 7E, with citations to Jumper et al., 2021; Varadi et al., 2022

claim: FLD2 showed degeneration of both the A5 and A7 motifs.
source: Structure-based sequence alignments, using models from AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (Jumper et al., 2021; Varadi et al., 2022), suggested that the A5 and A7 motifs are conserved in the FLD1 domains of all opisthokonts (Figure 7E) and strikingly, FLD2 showed degeneration of both the motifs.
evidence: Inferred from sequence alignment and shown in Figure 7E, with citations to Jumper et al., 2021; Varadi et al., 2022

claim: Mutations in catalytic residues of adenylation motifs of FLD1 led to the loss of function of ScDIP2.
source: Mutations in catalytic residues of adenylation motifs of FLD1 (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A) led to the loss of function of ScDIP2.
evidence: Measured by serial dilution assay and lipidomics

claim: Adenylation mutants of ScDIP2 failed to rescue the ∆ScDIP2 from tunicamycin-induced ER stress.
source: These adenylation mutants failed to rescue the ∆ScDIP2 from tunicamycin-induced ER stress (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D) and also showed an inability to regulate the levels of accumulated DAGs by converting them to related TAGs (Figure 7F, G).
evidence: Measured by serial dilution assay and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D

claim: Adenylation mutants of ScDIP2 showed an inability to regulate the levels of accumulated DAGs by converting them to related TAGs.
source: These adenylation mutants failed to rescue the ∆ScDIP2 from tunicamycin-induced ER stress (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D) and also showed an inability to regulate the levels of accumulated DAGs by converting them to related TAGs (Figure 7F, G).
evidence: Measured by LC-MS and shown in Figure 7F, G

claim: Overexpression of adenylation mutants of ScDIP2 did not result in fragmented vacuole morphology.
source: Overexpression of these mutants neither resulted in fragmented vacuole morphology nor an increased cell death in hypotonic stress condition as seen with wild-type ScDIP2 overexpression (Figure 7—figure supplement 2F, G).
evidence: Observed by fluorescence microscopy and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2F

claim: Overexpression of adenylation mutants of ScDIP2 did not result in increased cell death in hypotonic stress condition.
source: Overexpression of these mutants neither resulted in fragmented vacuole morphology nor an increased cell death in hypotonic stress condition as seen with wild-type ScDIP2 overexpression (Figure 7—figure supplement 2F, G).
evidence: Measured by trypan blue staining and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2G

claim: The expression and the localization pattern of FLD1 adenylation mutants were identical to the wild-type ScDIP2.
source: The expression and the localization pattern of FLD1 adenylation mutants were identical to the wild-type ScDIP2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: Observed by fluorescence microscopy and western blot, shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B, C

claim: The mutation of predicted residues of the degenerate motifs in FLD2 did not lead to the loss of function.
source: The mutation of predicted residues of the degenerate motifs in FLD2 did not lead to the loss of function (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B, C, E).
evidence: Measured by serial dilution assay and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B, C, E

claim: The adenylation activity of FLD1 of DIP2 is required for facilitating the conversion of selective DAGs to TAGs.
source: Taken together, the adenylation activity of FLD1 of DIP2 is required for facilitating the conversion of selective DAGs to TAGs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that adenylation mutants lose function

claim: FLD2 has not retained adenylation activity and has diverged for a yet to be identified function.
source: Also, it can be suggested that FLD2 has not retained adenylation activity and has diverged for a yet to be identified function.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that FLD2 motifs are degenerate and mutations do not affect function

claim: Total DAG pool constitutes only a relatively small population (3–5%) within the lipidome.
source: Total DAG pool constitutes only a relatively small population (3–5%) within the lipidome (Casanovas et al., 2015; Ejsing et al., 2009) and is maintained via the rapid turnover to either storage lipids or membrane lipids.
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations to Casanovas et al., 2015; Ejsing et al., 2009

claim: The deletion of DAG metabolizing enzymes of yeast such as Dgk1, Dga1 and Lro1 results in the accumulation of bulk DAG species.
source: Indeed, the deletion of DAG metabolizing enzymes of yeast such as Dgk1, which facilitates the formation of phospholipids, or Dga1 and Lro1, that facilitate TAG synthesis results in the accumulation of bulk DAG species (Fakas et al., 2011; Mora et al., 2012; Oelkers et al., 2002; Oelkers et al., 2000; Rockenfeller et al., 2018).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations to Fakas et al., 2011; Mora et al., 2012; Oelkers et al., 2002; Oelkers et al., 2000; Rockenfeller et al., 2018

claim: The accumulation of bulk DAGs in Dga1 or Lro1 or Dgk1 mutants does not lead to ER stress induction.
source: Surprisingly, unlike the DIP2 mutant which accumulates a subset of the DAG pool (<0.005%), the accumulation of bulk DAGs in Dga1 or Lro1 or Dgk1 mutants does not lead to ER stress induction.
evidence: Measured by serial dilution assay

claim: ScDIP2 is likely to have a limited effect on lipid droplet (LD) biogenesis process.
source: Since the levels of bulk TAG pools and sterol esters in ΔScDIP2 cells show minimal or no change, ScDIP2 is likely to have a limited effect on lipid droplet (LD) biogenesis process.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that bulk TAG and sterol ester levels are unchanged

claim: The minor DAG pool is resistant to any kind of redirection that retains them in the membrane.
source: The present study identifies the minor DAG pool as being resistant to any kind of redirection that retains them in the membrane.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that only DIP2 can regulate these DAGs

claim: These DAG subspecies can only be titrated as a storage lipid, TAG, by DIP2 in the logarithmic growth phase and via oleic acid-mediated 'metabolic reset' in the stationary phase.
source: These DAGs can only be titrated as a storage lipid, TAG, by DIP2 in the logarithmic growth phase and via oleic acid-mediated 'metabolic reset' in the stationary phase.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that DAG levels are restored by DIP2 in log phase and by OL in stationary phase

claim: The accumulation of these DAG subspecies is likely to impact the physical properties of the membrane, which subsequently results in UPR triggering and vacuole fusion dysregulation.
source: Thus, the accumulation of these DAG subspecies is likely to impact the physical properties of the membrane, which subsequently results in UPR triggering and vacuole fusion dysregulation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that DAG accumulation leads to ER stress and vacuole fusion defects

claim: DIP2-mediated fine-tuning of a fraction of the DAG pool is required for adapting to different types of stress such as ER proteostasis and osmolarity.
source: Overall, the current work shows that DIP2-mediated fine-tuning of a fraction of the DAG pool is required for adapting to different types of stress such as ER proteostasis and osmolarity.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that DIP2 mutants are sensitive to ER stress and osmotic stress

claim: Pathogenic fungi adapt to the changing microenvironments during disease progression.
source: As pathogenic fungi adapt to the changing microenvironments during disease progression, similar stress adaptation processes linked to DAG regulation becomes crucial for their survival inside the host.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field

claim: DIP2 is involved in infection-related morphogenesis like conidia, appressoria, hyphae, and spherule formation in pathogenic fungi.
source: Studies on plant and animal pathogenic fungi have indeed suggested that DIP2 is involved in infection-related morphogenesis like conidia, appressoria, hyphae, and spherule formation (Lu et al., 2003; Narra et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016), where vacuole fusion–fission dynamics plays a vital role (Veses et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 2003; Narra et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Veses et al., 2008

claim: Vacuole fusion–fission dynamics plays a vital role in infection-related morphogenesis in pathogenic fungi.
source: Studies on plant and animal pathogenic fungi have indeed suggested that DIP2 is involved in infection-related morphogenesis like conidia, appressoria, hyphae, and spherule formation (Lu et al., 2003; Narra et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016), where vacuole fusion–fission dynamics plays a vital role (Veses et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Veses et al., 2008

claim: DIP2 has been identified as a potential candidate for designing fungicides and developing a vaccine against valley fever.
source: Consequently, DIP2 has been identified as a potential candidate for designing fungicides and developing a vaccine against valley fever (Shubitz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shubitz et al., 2018

claim: DAG regulation in neurons is found as a critical factor for neuron branching and dendritic spine formation.
source: Furthermore, DAG regulation in neurons is found as a critical factor for neuron branching, dendritic spine formation (Tu-Sekine et al., 2015), etc., which are the major cellular processes affected in autism and related neurodevelopmental disorders (Gilbert and Man, 2017; Phillips and Pozzo-Miller, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tu-Sekine et al., 2015; Gilbert and Man, 2017; Phillips and Pozzo-Miller, 2015

claim: Neuron branching and dendritic spine formation are major cellular processes affected in autism and related neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Furthermore, DAG regulation in neurons is found as a critical factor for neuron branching, dendritic spine formation (Tu-Sekine et al., 2015), etc., which are the major cellular processes affected in autism and related neurodevelopmental disorders (Gilbert and Man, 2017; Phillips and Pozzo-Miller, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gilbert and Man, 2017; Phillips and Pozzo-Miller, 2015

claim: Aberrant accumulation of chemically distinct DAG subspecies is likely to be the potential molecular driver of autism and related neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Since DIP2 has been recognized as a potential risk factor for ASD and other neurodevelopmental disorders (Supplementary file 1), aberrant accumulation of chemically distinct DAG subspecies is likely to be the potential molecular driver of these disorders.
evidence: Speculated based on the role of DIP2 in DAG regulation

claim: FLD didomain of DIP2 is required for proper neuron branching in Drosophila and C. elegans.
source: Interestingly, the previous reports suggesting the requirement FLD didomain of DIP2 for proper neuron branching in Drosophila and C. elegans (Nitta et al., 2017; Noblett et al., 2019) correlates with our observation on the need of FLD didomain in selective DAG to TAG conversion.
evidence: Supported by citations to Nitta et al., 2017; Noblett et al., 2019

claim: DIP2 is possibly involved in driving crucial developmental processes via DAG subspecies regulation.
source: This also suggests the possible involvement of DIP2 in driving these crucial developmental processes via DAG subspecies regulation.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between FLD didomain requirement in neuron branching and DAG regulation
